title: Monitoring & The Deteriorating Patient
summary: How to read a bedside monitor honestly, spot the patient who is sliding hours before the alarm says so, say it out loud in twenty seconds, and know your job when the room turns into a code.

lessons.title: The bedside monitor: reading the screen
lessons.body:
## Five numbers and a few pictures

A bedside monitor is several separate instruments sharing one screen. Each one measures something different, by a different physical method, and each one fails in its own way. Knowing which is which is the difference between trusting a number and checking it.

Most monitors in United States emergency departments follow roughly the same color convention, though it varies by manufacturer and can be reconfigured by your department:

| Parameter | Usual color | What it actually measures |
|---|---|---|
| Heart rate and ECG | Green | Electrical activity from chest electrodes |
| SpO2 (oxygen saturation) | Blue or cyan | Light absorbed by blood in a finger or ear |
| NIBP (blood pressure) | Red or pink | Cuff pressure oscillations, measured in cycles |
| Respiratory rate | Yellow or white | Chest impedance change between ECG electrodes, or capnography |
| Temperature | White or grey | Probe, tympanic, oral or rectal |

> **Trap:** Learn your department's actual screen, not a color rule from a textbook. Different vendors and different units within one hospital use different schemes, and the one time you read the wrong row is the time it matters.

## Where each number comes from, and how it lies

The **heart rate** on most monitors is counted from the ECG, which means it counts electrical complexes, not heartbeats. Artifact, a tall T wave, or a shaking patient can all be counted as extra beats and double the displayed rate.

The **respiratory rate** on the green-yellow row is usually derived by impedance: the machine measures how the electrical resistance between two chest electrodes changes as the chest expands. A patient who is talking, shivering, or moving produces a respiratory rate that is pure fiction. This is why the displayed respiratory rate is the least trustworthy number on the screen.

**SpO2** needs pulsatile blood flow at the sensor. Cold hands, low blood pressure, and motion all break it.

**NIBP** is a snapshot taken every few minutes, not a continuous value. Between cycles the number on the screen may be ten minutes old.

> **Key:** The monitor reports what its sensors detect. Any number that surprises you gets confirmed by a human method — count the respirations yourself, feel the pulse, take a manual blood pressure.

## Setting the patient up

When you put someone on the monitor, do four things in order: prep and place the ECG electrodes, place the SpO2 probe on a warm perfused finger or ear, size and apply the blood pressure cuff, then set alarm limits appropriate to this patient rather than accepting defaults.

Then get a baseline set. A baseline is what makes every later number meaningful, because deterioration is a change, and you cannot see change without a starting point.

> **On shift:** Write down or chart the first full set the moment you get it, including a manually counted respiratory rate. The trend you build from that baseline is worth more than any single reading you will take all shift.
keyPoints: A monitor is several instruments sharing one screen, each failing in its own way.
Typical colors are green heart rate, blue or cyan SpO2, red or pink NIBP, yellow respiratory rate, white temperature — but they vary by vendor.
The displayed heart rate counts electrical complexes, and the displayed respiratory rate is derived from chest impedance, so both can be fiction.
NIBP is an intermittent snapshot; the number on screen may be minutes old.
Any surprising number gets confirmed by hand before anyone acts on it.

checks.q: The monitor shows a respiratory rate of 32 in a patient who is chatting comfortably with her daughter. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: She is in early respiratory failure
Impedance-derived respiratory rate is counting talking and movement
The SpO2 probe is on the wrong finger
The blood pressure cuff is too small
checks.why: Impedance respiratory rate measures chest wall movement between ECG electrodes, so speech and motion inflate it. Count the respirations yourself for 30 to 60 seconds before believing the screen.

checks.q: Why is the NIBP number on the screen not a continuous value?
choices: It is calculated from the SpO2 waveform
It is measured only when the cuff cycles, so it can be minutes old
It updates once per heartbeat
It is an average of the last hour
checks.why: Non-invasive blood pressure is taken in discrete cuff cycles. Between cycles the displayed value is simply the last measurement, which may no longer reflect the patient.

checks.q: What should you do immediately after placing a patient on the monitor?
choices: Accept the default alarm limits and move on
Set alarm limits for this patient and record a full baseline set including a counted respiratory rate
Silence all alarms until the provider sees the patient
Wait for the first automatic cycle before charting anything
checks.why: Deterioration is a change from baseline, so the baseline has to exist. Default limits are built for an average patient and are wrong for many real ones, and silencing alarms removes the safety net entirely.

lessons.title: Alarms: limits, fatigue, and what to do
lessons.body:
## Why alarms stop working

A busy emergency department generates hundreds of alarms per patient per day, and studies of hospital telemetry consistently find that the large majority — commonly cited as over 85% — are false or clinically insignificant. The predictable result is alarm fatigue: staff stop reacting, response times stretch, and the one real alarm arrives into a room full of people who have learned to tune it out.

Alarm fatigue is not an annoyance. It has killed patients, and it is why alarm management is a national patient safety priority.

> **Key:** Every false alarm you leave unfixed makes the next real alarm less likely to be answered. Fixing a curling electrode is clinical work.

## Defaults are wrong for some patients

A typical adult default might alarm at a heart rate under 50 or over 120, SpO2 under 90%, and systolic blood pressure under 90 or over 180. Those numbers are built for an average patient who does not exist.

- A patient with severe COPD may live at an SpO2 of `88%`. A default low limit of `90%` will alarm all night for a normal value, while a genuine drop to `82%` blends into the noise.
- A young athlete may sit comfortably at a heart rate of `46`.
- A patient in rapid atrial fibrillation who arrived at `150` and is being rate-controlled needs limits that track the goal, not the arrival number.
- A pediatric patient on adult default limits is effectively unmonitored, because a child's normal heart rate exceeds an adult's alarm threshold.

Limits get set for the patient in front of you, by the nurse or per department protocol, and they get re-set when the patient's condition changes.

## Silence, adjust, or escalate

Three different actions, and the difference matters.

**Silence** is appropriate when you have gone to the patient, seen that they are fine, and identified the cause — a lead off during a bed transfer, a cuff cycling while the arm is moving. Silence at the bedside, after looking, never from the desk.

**Adjust** is appropriate when the limit itself is wrong for this patient, and it is done by the nurse or per protocol, and documented. Widening a limit to quiet a mechanical problem is not adjusting; it is hiding.

**Escalate** is appropriate whenever the alarm reflects the patient: a new rhythm, a real desaturation, a real pressure drop, or anything you cannot explain within about thirty seconds.

> **Trap:** Never disable an alarm, never turn the volume to zero, and never widen limits so far that nothing can trigger them. If an alarm genuinely cannot be managed, that is a conversation with the nurse, not a knob you turn.

## The technician's alarm habits

Fix the mechanical causes at the source: fresh electrodes on dry skin, correct cuff size, warm perfused finger for the probe, cables with slack. Answer alarms you did not cause, because the person who can see the screen is responsible for the patient attached to it.

And say what you saw. The words a nurse needs are the parameter, the value, the trend and the patient: SpO2 dropped from `96%` to `88%` over ten minutes, he is using his neck muscles, room 8.

> **On shift:** If you silence an alarm without going to the room, you have made a clinical decision about a patient you have not seen. That is the one habit that ends careers.
keyPoints: The large majority of hospital monitor alarms are false or insignificant, which produces alarm fatigue and delayed responses.
Default limits are wrong for COPD patients, athletes, rate-controlled atrial fibrillation, and every child.
Silence only at the bedside after seeing the patient and identifying the cause.
Adjust limits only for the patient's real physiology, by the nurse or per protocol, and document it.
Never disable an alarm, zero the volume, or widen limits to hide a mechanical problem.

checks.q: A COPD patient's SpO2 alarms continuously at 88 to 89 percent, which the provider has documented as his baseline. What is the correct action?
choices: Turn off the SpO2 alarm
Ask the nurse to adjust the low SpO2 limit for this patient and document it
Remove the probe
Silence the alarm each time from the central station
checks.why: The limit is wrong for this patient's physiology, so the limit is what changes — by the nurse, documented. Disabling the alarm or removing the probe leaves him unmonitored, and repeated remote silencing means nobody ever looks at him.

checks.q: When is it appropriate to silence an alarm?
choices: From the desk, when the patient looked fine an hour ago
At the bedside, after seeing the patient and identifying the cause
Whenever the same alarm has fired more than three times
When the nurse is busy with another patient
checks.why: Silencing is a statement that you know why the alarm fired and that the patient is safe. You cannot know that from the desk, and repetition is not evidence of a false alarm.

checks.q: Why is alarm fatigue considered a patient safety problem rather than a nuisance?
choices: It wastes electricity
It shortens electrode life
Repeated false alarms train staff to ignore alarms, delaying response to real events
It makes documentation harder
checks.why: When most alarms are false, response times lengthen and real events get missed. That is a documented cause of patient deaths and the reason alarm management is a national safety priority.

lessons.title: Pulse oximetry: the waveform and the lies
lessons.body:
## How the number is made

A pulse oximeter shines two wavelengths of light — red and infrared — through a finger and measures how much comes out the other side. Blood carrying oxygen absorbs the two wavelengths differently from blood that is not, so the ratio gives a saturation percentage (SpO2).

The critical detail: the device only looks at the part of the signal that **pulses**. It subtracts everything steady — skin, bone, nail, venous blood — and reads only the arterial pulse wave. No pulse at the sensor means no reading, and a weak pulse means a bad reading.

## Read the waveform, not just the number

Every good monitor displays a plethysmograph (pleth) waveform beside the SpO2 number, or at minimum a signal quality bar. A good pleth wave is a clean, regular, sharp upstroke with a notch on the downslope, repeating with each heartbeat.

> **Key:** A saturation number without a clean pleth waveform is not a measurement. It is a guess. Look at the waveform every time before you chart or report the number.

Flat, ragged, or wildly irregular pleth means the sensor is not seeing arterial pulsation, and whatever number it displays is unreliable in either direction.

## What makes it read wrong

**Low perfusion.** Cold hands, shock, vasoconstrictors, peripheral vascular disease. The most common fix: warm the hand, move to a different finger, or move the probe to an ear lobe, forehead sensor, or toe per department stock.

**Motion.** Shivering, tremor, seizure, a patient tapping the rail. Motion is read as pulsation.

**Nail polish and artificial nails.** Dark colors, especially blue, green, black and brown, absorb the light. Remove the polish or turn the probe sideways so light passes through the sides of the finger.

**Carbon monoxide.** This is the dangerous one. Carboxyhemoglobin absorbs light almost identically to oxygenated hemoglobin, so a CO-poisoned patient can read `100%` while suffocating. A standard pulse oximeter cannot detect CO poisoning. Suspected exposure needs a CO-oximeter or a blood gas, and the history — a house fire, a generator in a garage, a whole family with headaches — is the finding.

**Methemoglobinemia** drags the reading toward roughly `85%` regardless of the true saturation.

Other causes of error: severe anemia (the saturation can be normal while total oxygen carried is dangerously low), intravenous dyes, and a blood pressure cuff cycling on the same arm as the probe.

## The patient who reads 98% and looks terrible

Saturation is one of four things that have to go right, and it only reports one of them: how full the hemoglobin is. It says nothing about how much hemoglobin exists, how much blood is moving, or how well carbon dioxide is being cleared.

This is why a patient with a normal SpO2 can still be in respiratory failure. Early on, a patient works harder — faster rate, accessory muscles in the neck, tripoding, short sentences — and keeps the saturation normal by brute effort. The saturation falls last, when the effort fails.

> **Trap:** Never let a normal SpO2 override what you see. Work of breathing, the ability to speak in full sentences, and mental status are earlier and better signals than the number.

> **On shift:** Report both: SpO2 is `97%` on room air, but he is breathing 30 times a minute with his neck muscles and can only say three words at a time.
keyPoints: Pulse oximetry reads only pulsating arterial blood, so it fails wherever perfusion fails.
A saturation number is only valid when the pleth waveform is clean and regular.
Carbon monoxide makes the oximeter read falsely high, often 100%; a standard probe cannot detect it.
Dark nail polish, motion, cold hands and a cuff on the same arm all corrupt the reading.
Work of breathing and mental status change before saturation does; a normal SpO2 never overrules how the patient looks.

checks.q: A firefighter pulled from a house fire is confused and headachy, with an SpO2 of 100% on room air. What is the concern?
choices: The probe is on the wrong finger
Carbon monoxide poisoning — carboxyhemoglobin makes the oximeter read falsely high
He is hyperventilating
Nothing; 100% is reassuring
checks.why: Carboxyhemoglobin absorbs light nearly identically to oxyhemoglobin, so a standard pulse oximeter reads high and cannot detect CO. Confusion plus a fire history needs a CO-oximeter or blood gas, not reassurance.

checks.q: The SpO2 reads 84% but the pleth waveform is flat and ragged and the patient's hand is cold. What do you do first?
choices: Report a critical desaturation immediately
Apply oxygen at 15 L/min by non-rebreather
Warm the hand or move the probe to another site and look for a clean waveform
Chart 84% and recheck in an hour
checks.why: Without a clean pleth wave there is no valid measurement, and low perfusion is the classic cause. Get a real reading first, while still looking at the patient. Charting a bad number or acting on it can be equally wrong.

checks.q: A patient breathing 30 times a minute using neck muscles has an SpO2 of 97%. What does this mean?
choices: He is compensating, and saturation falls last when that effort fails
He is fine because the saturation is normal
The probe is reading falsely high
He needs no reassessment for an hour
checks.why: Increased work of breathing keeps saturation normal until the patient tires. The normal number is the result of effort, not the absence of a problem, and it will drop suddenly when compensation ends.

lessons.title: Capnography: the vital sign that moves first
lessons.body:
## What EtCO2 measures

Capnography measures carbon dioxide in exhaled breath. End-tidal CO2 (EtCO2) is the value at the very end of an exhalation, when the sampled gas is coming from deep in the lungs.

Normal is `35-45 mmHg`, and it is normally within a few mmHg of arterial CO2.

That one number depends on three things happening: the body producing CO2 (metabolism), the blood carrying it to the lungs (circulation), and the lungs blowing it off (ventilation). Break any of the three and EtCO2 changes — which is exactly why it moves before the other numbers do.

> **Key:** SpO2 tells you about oxygen going in. EtCO2 tells you about carbon dioxide coming out, and about whether blood is moving at all. Ventilation fails before oxygenation does, so EtCO2 falls or rises minutes before the saturation moves.

## The normal waveform

A normal capnogram is a rectangle with four phases: a flat baseline at zero as the breath begins (dead space gas, no CO2), a rapid upstroke as alveolar gas arrives, a flat plateau ending in the end-tidal peak, then a sharp fall back to zero as the next breath is drawn in.

The shape matters as much as the number.

- **Shark fin** — the upstroke slurs into a rising slope with no flat plateau. This is obstruction: asthma or COPD bronchospasm. The shape improves as a bronchodilator works, often before the patient reports feeling better.
- **Baseline that does not return to zero** — rebreathing CO2, or a problem with the circuit or valves.
- **A sudden flat line at zero** — no exhaled CO2 at all: a disconnected circuit, a dislodged tube, complete obstruction, or cardiac arrest.

## Confirming an advanced airway

Waveform capnography is the standard for confirming and continuously monitoring placement of an endotracheal tube. A sustained, normally shaped waveform over several breaths means the tube is in the trachea. An esophageal tube gives no waveform, or a couple of small deflections that disappear.

If the waveform disappears at any point after placement, the tube has moved, the circuit has come apart, or the patient has arrested. It is checked, not assumed.

## EtCO2 in cardiac arrest

This is the one every ED technician should know cold, because it is the direct feedback on the work your arms are doing.

During CPR, the lungs are ventilated but blood only reaches them if compressions are moving it. So EtCO2 during arrest is a measure of **compression quality and cardiac output**.

- EtCO2 persistently under `10 mmHg` during CPR means the compressions are not generating enough flow. Push harder, push faster, allow full chest recoil, and swap the compressor.
- A sudden sustained rise to over `40 mmHg` — often a jump from 12 to 45 within a couple of breaths — usually means return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC). Blood is suddenly moving again and delivering a backlog of CO2 to the lungs. Check a pulse at the next rhythm check.
- After 20 minutes of resuscitation, an EtCO2 that stays under `10 mmHg` is one of several factors associated with a very poor outcome and is used, with everything else, in decisions about stopping.

> **On shift:** When a code leader says what is the end-tidal, they are asking whether the compressions are working. That number is feedback on you, and the honest answer improves the next two minutes.

> **Trap:** Do not confuse a rise in EtCO2 from ROSC with a rise from giving sodium bicarbonate, which also raises it briefly. Correlate with a pulse check and the rhythm.

## Other uses

Nasal-cannula capnography is used on sedated patients, overdoses and procedural sedation, where it detects apnea within seconds — long before the pulse oximeter, especially if the patient is on supplemental oxygen. A rising EtCO2 with a slowing rate is the early signature of opioid-induced respiratory depression. A low EtCO2 with a fast rate can point to severe metabolic acidosis, such as diabetic ketoacidosis, where the patient is deliberately blowing off CO2.
keyPoints: Normal EtCO2 is 35-45 mmHg and reflects metabolism, circulation and ventilation together.
The waveform shape matters: a shark fin means bronchospasm, a sudden flat line means disconnection, dislodgement or arrest.
Waveform capnography is the standard for confirming and continuously monitoring an endotracheal tube.
During CPR, EtCO2 under 10 mmHg means fix the compressions; a sudden sustained rise over 40 mmHg suggests ROSC.
On sedated patients, capnography detects apnea long before pulse oximetry, especially on supplemental oxygen.

checks.q: During CPR the EtCO2 reads 7 mmHg. What does this tell the team?
choices: The patient has ROSC
The tube is in the esophagus
Compressions are not generating enough blood flow — push harder and faster, allow full recoil, swap the compressor
The monitor needs recalibration
checks.why: EtCO2 during arrest is a direct measure of the cardiac output your compressions produce. Under 10 mmHg means inadequate flow. ROSC produces a sudden rise above 40, and an esophageal tube produces no waveform at all.

checks.q: An asthmatic patient's capnogram shows a slurred upstroke with no flat plateau. What is this and what does it mean?
choices: A shark fin pattern indicating bronchospasm
Rebreathing from a faulty valve
Esophageal intubation
Normal for an adult
checks.why: Obstruction makes alveoli empty at different rates, so the plateau never flattens, producing the shark fin. It improves as bronchodilators work, often before the patient feels better. Rebreathing raises the baseline off zero instead.

checks.q: Why does EtCO2 detect deterioration earlier than SpO2 in a sedated patient on oxygen?
choices: EtCO2 sensors are more accurate
Supplemental oxygen keeps saturation normal for minutes after breathing stops, while exhaled CO2 changes within seconds
SpO2 only updates every five minutes
EtCO2 measures brain function
checks.why: An oxygen reservoir in the lungs holds saturation up well after ventilation stops, so the oximeter alarms late. Capnography reports each breath, so apnea shows immediately.

lessons.title: Blood pressure, cuffs, and reassessment intervals
lessons.body:
## How the machine gets the number

Non-invasive blood pressure (NIBP) works by oscillometry. The cuff inflates above systolic pressure, then bleeds down while a sensor feels the tiny pressure oscillations transmitted from the artery. The point of maximum oscillation is the mean arterial pressure, which the machine measures directly; it then calculates systolic and diastolic from that using the manufacturer's algorithm.

That is worth knowing because the mean is the measured value and the systolic is derived. In shock, atrial fibrillation, severe tremor and extreme hypertension, the derived numbers drift from truth while the mean stays more reliable.

## Cuff size is not a detail

The bladder inside the cuff should span roughly `80%` of the arm circumference and about `40%` of the arm width, with the artery marker over the brachial artery and the lower edge about `2-3 cm` above the antecubital crease.

- A cuff that is **too small** reads falsely **high**. This is the common error, and it produces fake hypertension and unnecessary workups.
- A cuff that is **too large** reads falsely **low**, which is far more dangerous because it can mask real hypertension or, in the other direction, trigger an unnecessary intervention.

The arm should be supported at heart level. An arm hanging down reads high; an arm held above the heart reads low. Roughly `10 mmHg` of error per `13 cm` of height difference.

> **Key:** When a blood pressure surprises you, take it manually before anyone acts on it. Wrong cuff, wrong arm position, movement and a cycling cuff on a moving patient produce most of the surprises.

## Cycling, and what it costs

Automatic cycling at `5` or `15` minute intervals is standard. Cycling every `1-2 minutes` for long periods bruises, causes petechiae, and can cause nerve pain or compartment problems — reserve it for short, actively managed periods.

Do not put the cuff on an arm with a dialysis fistula or graft, on the side of a mastectomy with lymph node dissection, on a limb with an infusing IV or a PICC line, or on an injured or casted limb. Move to the other arm, or use a thigh cuff on the leg with an appropriately larger size, and tell the nurse where you took it.

## When to confirm by hand

Confirm manually when: the reading is much higher or lower than the last one with no clinical change, the patient looks different from the number, the machine reports an error or repeats the cycle, the patient is in atrial fibrillation or shivering, or a treatment decision is about to be made on that number.

For a palpated pressure, inflate while feeling the radial pulse, note where it disappears, then deflate slowly — that gives a systolic only, and it is enough in an emergency.

## How often to recheck

Intervals vary by department protocol and acuity level, but a common pattern using the five-level Emergency Severity Index is:

| Acuity | Typical vitals interval |
|---|---|
| ESI 1 (resuscitation) | Continuous monitoring, documented every `5 minutes` |
| ESI 2 (emergent) | Every `15 minutes`, continuous monitoring |
| ESI 3 (urgent) | Every `30-60 minutes` |
| ESI 4-5 (less urgent) | Every `1-4 hours`, and at discharge |

On top of the schedule, repeat a full set: after any medication that can change vital signs, after any intervention, any time the patient's appearance or complaint changes, before transport off the unit, before discharge, and whenever something makes you uneasy.

> **On shift:** Continuous monitoring does not replace laying hands on a patient. Somebody has to touch the skin, count the breaths, and look at the face. The monitor cannot see mottled knees or a patient who has stopped talking.
keyPoints: NIBP measures mean arterial pressure directly and calculates systolic and diastolic from it.
A cuff too small reads falsely high; a cuff too large reads falsely low. Bladder spans about 80% of arm circumference.
Avoid the cuff on a fistula or graft arm, a mastectomy side with node dissection, a limb with an infusing IV, or an injured limb.
Confirm manually when the number surprises you, before any treatment decision is made on it.
Typical intervals: ESI 1 every 5 minutes, ESI 2 every 15, ESI 3 every 30-60, ESI 4-5 every 1-4 hours, plus after every intervention or change.

checks.q: A blood pressure cuff that is too small for the arm will:
choices: Read falsely low
Read falsely high
Fail to inflate
Read the mean accurately but not the systolic
checks.why: A small cuff needs excessive pressure to compress the artery, so the reported pressure is too high. A cuff that is too large reads falsely low, which is the more dangerous error because it can mask hypertension.

checks.q: A patient with a left arm dialysis fistula and a right arm IV infusing needs a blood pressure. What do you do?
choices: Use the fistula arm; it is only a cuff
Stop the IV and use the right arm
Use an appropriately sized thigh cuff on a leg and document the site
Skip the blood pressure
checks.why: A fistula or graft arm is never cuffed, and cuffing over an infusing IV interrupts the infusion and gives an unreliable reading. A correctly sized lower extremity cuff is the standard alternative, and the site gets documented so readings are compared fairly.

checks.q: What is a typical vitals interval for an ESI level 2 patient?
choices: Every 15 minutes with continuous monitoring
Every 2 hours
Once at triage and once at discharge
Every 4 hours
checks.why: ESI 2 patients are emergent and high risk, so they are continuously monitored with documented sets about every 15 minutes. Hourly or longer intervals belong to lower acuity levels, and intervals shorten any time the patient changes.

lessons.title: Catching deterioration early
lessons.body:
## Patients do not crash without warning

Reviews of in-hospital cardiac arrests find that the majority of patients showed abnormal vital signs in the hours beforehand — most often a rising respiratory rate, a falling blood pressure, or a change in mental status. The signs were there. They were recorded. Nobody put them together.

That is the job this lesson is about. You take more sets of vital signs than anyone else in the department, which means you are the person most likely to see the trend first.

> **Key:** A single value tells you where the patient is. A trend tells you where the patient is going. Four readings drifting the same direction beat one abnormal number every time.

## Respiratory rate is the most ignored vital sign

It is the earliest and most sensitive marker of deterioration, and it is the one most often guessed, copied forward, or charted as 16 or 18 because that looks normal. A rate that climbs from 16 to 22 to 28 across three sets is a patient in trouble, even if every other number is unremarkable.

Count it. Thirty seconds doubled, or a full minute if it is irregular, with your hand on the wrist so the patient does not consciously change it.

## Numbers that mean trouble

**Shock index** = heart rate divided by systolic blood pressure. Normal is roughly `0.5-0.7`. A value **over `0.9`** predicts serious illness, transfusion need and mortality better than either number alone. A heart rate of `110` with a systolic of `110` gives an index of `1.0` — both numbers look almost acceptable, and the patient is in compensated shock.

**Narrowing pulse pressure** — the gap between systolic and diastolic. A pressure falling from `120/70` to `100/85` is a vasoconstricting patient losing volume, even though the systolic is still over 90.

**Urine output under `0.5 mL/kg/h`** — roughly under `30 mL/h` for an average adult. Kidneys stop making urine when perfusion drops, so falling output is an early organ-level warning.

**Capillary refill over `3 seconds`** and **mottling** — that blotchy blue-purple net over the knees and thighs. Mottling that spreads from the knee outward is a strong marker of severe shock and poor outcome.

## The things that are not numbers

**New confusion or agitation** in any patient is a vital sign. The brain is exquisitely sensitive to poor perfusion and low oxygen, and confusion often precedes any change on the monitor.

**Diaphoresis** — cool, clammy, sweaty skin in a patient who is not hot — means a catecholamine surge. The body is fighting something.

**The patient who says they want to sleep now**, or that something is wrong, or who suddenly goes quiet after being talkative. Patients who report a feeling of impending doom are frequently right. Withdrawal into sleep during an acute illness is not rest; it is a falling level of consciousness.

> **Trap:** Reassurance is not a plan. He is just tired, she is anxious, that is his baseline — each of those is a hypothesis, and none of them can be confirmed from the hallway. Say it to the nurse and let a clinician decide.

## How to voice it

The gut feeling is real data, but it only helps if you convert it into something a nurse can act on. Pair the feeling with the observation:

- Weak: I think something is off with room 8.
- Strong: Room 8, her respiratory rate went 18, 22, 26 over 45 minutes, systolic dropped from 128 to 96, and she is not answering me the way she was an hour ago. Can you come look?

That second version takes twelve seconds, contains a trend, a number and a mental status change, and it is nearly impossible to wave off.

> **On shift:** You are never wrong for asking a nurse to look at a patient. The only wrong version is the one where you noticed and said nothing.
keyPoints: Most in-hospital arrests are preceded by hours of abnormal vitals that were recorded but not connected.
Respiratory rate is the earliest and most-ignored warning sign — count it, never estimate it.
Shock index (HR divided by systolic) over 0.9 signals serious illness even when both numbers look acceptable.
Urine output under 0.5 mL/kg/h, cap refill over 3 seconds, mottling, diaphoresis and new confusion are all early organ-level warnings.
Voice concerns as trend plus number plus observation, not as a feeling.

checks.q: A patient has a heart rate of 112 and a blood pressure of 106/68. What is the shock index and what does it suggest?
choices: About 1.06 — elevated, suggesting compensated shock
About 0.6 — normal
About 1.6 — normal for this age
It cannot be calculated without a temperature
checks.why: Shock index is heart rate divided by systolic pressure: 112 divided by 106 is about 1.06. Normal is roughly 0.5 to 0.7, and anything over 0.9 predicts serious illness better than either number alone, even when both look nearly acceptable.

checks.q: Why is respiratory rate described as the most ignored vital sign?
choices: It rarely changes in illness
It is the earliest marker of deterioration but is often estimated or copied forward as a normal-looking number
Monitors measure it perfectly, so nobody needs to count
It only matters in asthma
checks.why: Respiratory rate rises before heart rate and blood pressure change, but it is routinely charted as 16 or 18 without counting, and impedance-derived monitor values are unreliable. Counting it for a full 30 to 60 seconds is what makes it useful.

checks.q: Which statement to a nurse is most likely to get a patient looked at promptly?
choices: Something feels off about room 8
Room 8 seems anxious
Room 8: respiratory rate went 18 to 22 to 26 over 45 minutes, systolic 128 down to 96, and she is less responsive than an hour ago
Room 8 asked for a blanket
checks.why: A trend with real numbers plus a mental status change is specific, verifiable and hard to defer. A bare feeling gives the nurse nothing to prioritize against the other patients competing for her attention.

lessons.title: Sepsis screening and calling for help
lessons.body:
## Why sepsis is screened by numbers

Sepsis is a dysregulated response to infection that injures the patient's own organs. It kills through time: mortality climbs measurably for every hour that antibiotics and fluids are delayed. Because early sepsis looks like a hundred other things, hospitals screen with simple number-based tools that a technician can apply from a vitals set.

> **Key:** You are not diagnosing sepsis. You are noticing that a set of numbers crosses a threshold, and saying so out loud within seconds.

## SIRS criteria

The oldest screen, still embedded in many hospital sepsis alerts. Two or more of:

- Temperature over `38 C` (`100.4 F`) or under `36 C` (`96.8 F`)
- Heart rate over `90`
- Respiratory rate over `20` (or PaCO2 under `32 mmHg`)
- White blood cell count over `12,000`/microliter, under `4,000`, or more than 10% immature bands

SIRS is sensitive and not specific — a bad flu or a marathon meets it. Two SIRS criteria plus a suspected infection is a reason to speak up, not a diagnosis.

## qSOFA

A bedside screen needing no labs. One point each for:

- Respiratory rate `22` or higher
- Altered mentation (any change from the patient's normal)
- Systolic blood pressure `100 mmHg` or lower

Two or more points identifies patients with infection at much higher risk of dying. qSOFA is less sensitive than SIRS for early sepsis but far more specific for a bad outcome — so a qSOFA of 2 is a loud alarm, while a qSOFA of 0 does not clear anyone.

## NEWS2

A scored early warning system used across many hospitals. Points are assigned for respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, whether supplemental oxygen is in use, systolic blood pressure, pulse, level of consciousness and temperature. In common use:

| Score | Typical response |
|---|---|
| `0-4` | Routine monitoring |
| `3` in any single parameter | Urgent review by a nurse |
| `5-6` | Urgent clinician review, escalate |
| `7` or more | Emergency response, continuous monitoring |

The important habit is not memorizing the table. It is knowing that one very abnormal parameter counts as much as several mildly abnormal ones.

## The sepsis bundle clock

When sepsis is suspected, a time-limited bundle starts, commonly targeted within `1 hour` for the hour-1 bundle: measure lactate, draw **blood cultures before antibiotics**, give broad-spectrum antibiotics, start `30 mL/kg` crystalloid for hypotension or lactate `4 mmol/L` or higher, and add vasopressors if pressure stays low. Repeat the lactate if the first was elevated.

Your part is usually the cultures, the IV, the point-of-care lactate, and the vitals. The one rule that must not slip: cultures go before antibiotics whenever drawing them will not delay the drug meaningfully.

## Calling a rapid response

Every hospital has a rapid response or medical emergency team, and in almost every hospital any staff member may activate it. Know your department's number and phrase before you need it.

Say it in about twenty seconds, in this order:

1. Who and where: This is Jose, ED technician, room 8.
2. The patient: 64-year-old woman, here for abdominal pain.
3. The concern, with numbers: Respiratory rate 28, systolic 88, temp `38.9 C`, and she is confused now — she was oriented an hour ago.
4. The ask: I need someone at the bedside now.

> **Trap:** Do not soften it. Maybe when you get a chance, if you are not busy, it might be nothing — these phrases get the patient deferred. State the numbers and ask for a person at the bedside.

> **On shift:** Escalating and being wrong costs three minutes of somebody's time. Not escalating and being wrong costs a life. Every rapid response system in the country is built around that arithmetic, and nobody gets disciplined for calling.
keyPoints: SIRS: two or more of temp over 38 C or under 36 C, HR over 90, RR over 20, WBC over 12k or under 4k.
qSOFA: one point each for RR 22 or more, altered mentation, systolic 100 or less; two points marks high risk of death.
NEWS2 scores seven parameters; a single parameter scoring 3 escalates just as a total of 5-6 does.
Hour-1 sepsis bundle: lactate, blood cultures before antibiotics, broad-spectrum antibiotics, 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate 4 or higher.
Any staff member can call a rapid response: name and location, patient, numbers, and a direct ask for someone at the bedside.

checks.q: A patient with a suspected urinary infection has a respiratory rate of 24, a systolic of 94, and is newly confused. What is the qSOFA score?
checks.why: One point each for respiratory rate 22 or higher, altered mentation, and systolic 100 or lower — all three are met, so the score is 3. Two or more identifies a markedly elevated risk of dying and needs immediate escalation.

checks.q: In the hour-1 sepsis bundle, what must happen before antibiotics are given?
choices: A chest X-ray
Blood cultures are drawn
A urinalysis results
The second lactate
checks.why: Antibiotics sterilize the blood within minutes, so cultures drawn afterward may never identify the organism. Cultures go first whenever obtaining them does not meaningfully delay the drug. Imaging and urinalysis are useful but never hold antibiotics.

checks.q: Which is the correct way to activate a rapid response?
choices: Tell the charge nurse you will keep an eye on the patient
Name and location, the patient, the abnormal numbers, and a direct request for someone at the bedside now
Wait for the next scheduled vitals to confirm the trend
Ask another technician whether it seems serious
checks.why: A rapid response call needs to be short, specific and unambiguous so the team can triage it instantly. Waiting for confirmation or polling colleagues burns the minutes the system exists to save, and any staff member is authorized to call.

lessons.title: The code blue as a technician
lessons.body:
## The first two minutes, when you are alone

You find a patient unresponsive. In order, taking seconds:

1. **Check responsiveness and breathing.** Shout and shake. Look for normal breathing — gasping (agonal respiration) is not breathing.
2. **Call for help** — pull the code button, shout for a nurse, activate the code team. Do not leave the room to find someone.
3. **Check a carotid pulse for no more than 10 seconds.** Checking pulse and breathing at the same time is fine.
4. **If no definite pulse, start compressions immediately.** The floor or a backboard, not a soft mattress.
5. **Attach the defibrillator or AED as soon as it arrives** and follow the prompts or the code leader.

## Compressions that actually work

These numbers matter more than anything else in the room:

- Rate `100-120` per minute
- Depth at least `2 inches` (`5 cm`), not more than `2.4 inches` (`6 cm`) in an adult
- **Full chest recoil** between compressions — leaning on the chest prevents the heart from refilling
- Minimize interruptions; aim for a chest compression fraction over `60%`, ideally over `80%`
- Compression to ventilation ratio `30:2` without an advanced airway; with an advanced airway, continuous compressions and one breath every `6 seconds` (10 per minute)
- **Swap compressors every 2 minutes**, at the rhythm check, in under `5 seconds`

The 2-minute swap is not a courtesy. Measured compression quality degrades within a minute or two, long before the person doing it feels tired.

> **Key:** Push hard, push fast, let the chest come all the way back up, and do not stop. Interruptions kill more than any other correctable error in a code.

## The roles a technician fills

**Compressor.** The default, and the most important.

**Timer and recorder.** Call out the 2-minute cycle, announce rhythm checks, track epinephrine intervals, write down times and doses. In many departments this is a technician role, and it is what makes the record and the drug timing correct.

**Defibrillator pads and charging.** Pads go on dry, bare skin, anterolateral: one right of the upper sternum below the clavicle, one at the left mid-axillary line over the 5th to 6th intercostal space. Avoid implanted devices and medication patches — remove patches and wipe the skin. Charge only when directed, announce clearly, ensure everyone including the person with oxygen is clear, then the licensed operator shocks. Compressions continue while the device charges and resume immediately after the shock.

**Medication runner.** Get what is called for and hand it to the nurse. You do not draw or push drugs.

**Backboard, crash cart, and door.** Slide the board, bring the cart, keep the doorway clear, run specimens.

## The crash cart

Layout varies, but the standard arrangement is airway on top, drugs in the first drawers, fluids and procedure supplies below. Recognizing the callouts is what lets you hand over the right box.

| Drug | Typical adult dose in arrest or peri-arrest |
|---|---|
| Epinephrine `1 mg` `1:10,000` | IV/IO every `3-5 minutes` during arrest |
| Amiodarone | `300 mg` IV, then `150 mg` for refractory VF/pulseless VT |
| Lidocaine | Alternative to amiodarone, `1-1.5 mg/kg` |
| Adenosine | `6 mg` rapid IV push, then `12 mg` for stable SVT |
| Atropine `1 mg` | Symptomatic bradycardia, repeat to `3 mg` total |
| Dextrose 50% (D50) | Hypoglycemia |
| Naloxone | Opioid overdose |
| Calcium chloride | Hyperkalemia, calcium channel blocker overdose |
| Sodium bicarbonate | Hyperkalemia, specific overdoses, prolonged arrest |
| Magnesium sulfate | Torsades de pointes |

The cart also holds defibrillator pads, a bag-valve mask and airway kit with laryngoscope, endotracheal and supraglottic airways, suction, IV and intraosseous (IO) supplies including the IO drill, and fluids.

## Mechanical CPR and EtCO2

Many departments have a mechanical compression device such as a LUCAS. It is positioned during a brief pause, suction cup over the lower half of the sternum, and delivers a fixed rate and depth without fatigue. Placement must not interrupt CPR for more than a few seconds.

Waveform capnography runs throughout: under `10 mmHg` means improve the compressions, and a sudden sustained jump over `40 mmHg` suggests return of spontaneous circulation.

## After ROSC

Typical immediate tasks: a **12-lead ECG** looking for STEMI, blood pressure support with frequent cycling, temperature measurement and targeted temperature management per protocol, airway and capnography confirmation, more access and labs, a chest X-ray, then monitored transport to the cath lab or ICU.

> **On shift:** Learn where your department's crash cart, defibrillator, backboard and IO drill live on your first shift. In a code, the person who knows where things are is worth two people who do not.
keyPoints: First two minutes alone: check responsiveness and breathing, call for help, pulse check under 10 seconds, start compressions, attach the defibrillator.
Compressions: rate 100-120, depth 2 to 2.4 inches, full recoil, 30:2 without an advanced airway, swap compressors every 2 minutes in under 5 seconds.
Pads go anterolateral on dry bare skin; compressions continue while charging and resume immediately after the shock.
Key callouts: epinephrine 1 mg every 3-5 minutes, amiodarone 300 mg then 150 mg, adenosine 6 mg then 12 mg, atropine 1 mg to a 3 mg maximum.
Post-ROSC: 12-lead ECG, blood pressure support, temperature management, airway and capnography confirmation, transport to cath lab or ICU.

checks.q: What is the correct adult compression rate and depth?
choices: 80-100 per minute, 1 to 1.5 inches
100-120 per minute, at least 2 inches and no more than 2.4 inches
120-140 per minute, 3 inches
60-80 per minute, as deep as possible
checks.why: Current AHA guidance is 100 to 120 per minute at a depth of 2 to 2.4 inches in an adult, with full recoil. Slower or shallower compressions generate too little flow, and excessive depth causes injury without added benefit.

checks.q: Why are compressors swapped every 2 minutes?
choices: To rotate who is exposed to body fluids
Measured compression quality falls within a minute or two, before the compressor feels tired
To give the defibrillator time to charge
Hospital policy requires equal participation
checks.why: Depth and recoil degrade quickly and the person compressing is the last to notice. The swap happens at the rhythm check and should take under 5 seconds so the compression fraction stays high.

checks.q: During a code the leader asks for the end-tidal and it reads 8 mmHg. What does the team do?
choices: Declare ROSC and check a pulse
Give sodium bicarbonate
Improve compression quality: push harder and faster, ensure full recoil, and swap the compressor
Stop the resuscitation immediately
checks.why: EtCO2 under 10 mmHg during CPR means the compressions are not moving enough blood. ROSC produces a sudden sustained rise above 40. A single low value is never by itself a reason to stop.

lessons.title: The patients you watch closely
lessons.body:
## Sedated and intubated patients

A patient who is sedated cannot protect their own airway, cannot tell you they are in pain, and cannot call for help. Everything that keeps them safe is something someone else does.

**Depth of sedation** is scored with the Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale (RASS), which runs from `+4` (combative) through `0` (alert and calm) down to `-5` (unarousable). Most sedated ED patients are targeted around `0 to -2` — drowsy but rousable — rather than deeply sedated, because deeper sedation prolongs ventilation and worsens outcomes. Report the number as the scale defines it: he is a minus 4, he only opens his eyes to physical stimulation.

**Head of bed at `30 degrees`** unless contraindicated, to reduce the chance of aspiration and ventilator-associated pneumonia.

**Ventilator alarms are respiratory therapy's call, not yours.** A high-pressure alarm often means a kink, biting, secretions or coughing; a low-pressure alarm often means a disconnection or a cuff leak. Your job is to look at the patient, check the obvious — tubing disconnected, patient biting, patient waking — and call respiratory therapy and the nurse. Do not change ventilator settings, ever.

**Suction awareness.** Know where the suction is, that it is connected and working, and that a Yankauer and a suction catheter are at the bedside for every sedated or intubated patient. Gurgling is an emergency you can hear from the hallway.

**Restraints** are a last resort, require an order, and carry their own monitoring: circulation checks distal to each restraint, skin checks, range of motion, offering food, fluids and toileting, and documentation at the interval your policy sets — commonly every `15 minutes` for violent or self-destructive restraint. Restrained patients are never left unobserved, and a restrained patient who becomes quiet gets checked immediately rather than left alone.

## Neuro checks and the stroke patient

The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) scores eye opening (`1-4`), verbal response (`1-5`) and motor response (`1-6`), totaling `3` to `15`. The trend is the point. A drop of `2` or more points is reported immediately.

**Pupils**: PERRL means pupils equal, round, reactive to light. A new unequal pupil, a sluggish pupil, or a blown pupil is an emergency and is reported the moment you see it.

The **NIHSS** is the formal stroke severity scale, scored by trained clinicians. You are not scoring it, but you will hear the number and you should know that higher means worse and that it is repeated to track change.

After thrombolytics (clot-busting drugs such as alteplase or tenecteplase), protocols typically call for neuro checks and blood pressure **every `15 minutes` for the first 2 hours**, then every 30 minutes for 6 hours, then hourly. Blood pressure is kept under a strict ceiling, commonly `180/105`, because the drug plus high pressure risks bleeding into the brain.

> **Key:** During a post-thrombolytic watch, a new headache, nausea and vomiting, sudden hypertension, or any decline in the neuro exam means intracranial bleeding until proven otherwise. Stop and get the nurse immediately.

## Pediatric monitoring

Children compensate beautifully and then fall off a cliff. Normal ranges by age:

| Age | Heart rate | Respiratory rate | Systolic BP |
|---|---|---|---|
| Newborn | `100-180` | `30-60` | `60-90` |
| Infant (1-12 mo) | `100-160` | `25-50` | `70-100` |
| Toddler (1-3 y) | `90-150` | `20-30` | `80-110` |
| Preschool (3-5 y) | `80-140` | `20-25` | `80-110` |
| School age (6-12 y) | `70-120` | `18-25` | `85-120` |
| Adolescent | `60-100` | `12-20` | `100-130` |

Three rules ride on top of that table:

1. **Bradycardia in a child is hypoxia until proven otherwise.** An adult's heart slows from cardiac causes; a child's slows because they are running out of oxygen, and it is a pre-arrest sign.
2. **Hypotension is a very late finding.** A child maintains blood pressure by clamping down until they suddenly cannot. Tachycardia, poor perfusion and lethargy come first.
3. **Everything is weight-based**, so an accurate weight in kilograms, or a length-based tape, is a safety item, not paperwork.

## Who you never leave alone

Some patients get eyes on them continuously: anyone actively suicidal or on a psychiatric hold, anyone in restraints, anyone sedated or post-procedure who is not fully awake, anyone with an unprotected airway or active vomiting, a patient actively seizing, an unstable patient waiting on transport, a patient in a hallway bed who is deteriorating, and an agitated patient who could hurt themselves or someone else.

> **On shift:** If you have to leave one of these patients, you hand the watch to a named person out loud and get an acknowledgment. Assuming someone is watching is how patients are found down.
keyPoints: RASS runs +4 to -5 with most sedated ED patients targeted around 0 to -2; head of bed at 30 degrees unless contraindicated.
Ventilator alarms mean look at the patient and call respiratory therapy — never change settings.
Restraints require an order, distal circulation and skin checks, and typically 15-minute documentation; restrained patients are never unobserved.
After thrombolytics, neuro checks and blood pressure every 15 minutes for 2 hours; new headache, vomiting or decline means bleeding until proven otherwise.
Bradycardia in a child is hypoxia until proven otherwise, and hypotension is a very late sign.

checks.q: A 3-year-old with pneumonia has a heart rate that falls from 160 to 70. What does this mean?
choices: He is improving and resting
Bradycardia in a child is hypoxia until proven otherwise — this is a pre-arrest sign requiring immediate help
It is normal for his age
The monitor is miscounting
checks.why: Children raise heart rate to compensate and slow only when oxygen delivery fails. A normal age range for a toddler is 90 to 150, so 70 in a sick child is a pre-arrest emergency, not rest.

checks.q: A patient two hours after thrombolytics for stroke develops a sudden severe headache and vomits. What is the concern?
choices: A medication side effect that will pass
Intracranial hemorrhage — stop and get the nurse immediately
Dehydration
Migraine
checks.why: New headache, vomiting, sudden hypertension or any neuro decline after thrombolytics means bleeding into the brain until proven otherwise. That is why neuro checks run every 15 minutes for the first 2 hours.

checks.q: A ventilator high-pressure alarm sounds on an intubated patient. What do you do?
choices: Adjust the pressure limit on the ventilator
Disconnect the circuit to relieve the pressure
Look at the patient, check for obvious causes like biting or kinked tubing, and call respiratory therapy and the nurse
Silence it and document
checks.why: Ventilator settings are changed only by respiratory therapy or a provider. Your role is to assess the patient, identify obvious mechanical causes, and escalate. Disconnecting the circuit or silencing the alarm endangers the patient.

cards.front: What does the heart rate on a bedside monitor actually count?
cards.back: Electrical complexes from the ECG, not heartbeats. Artifact, tall T waves or a shaking patient can all be counted as beats and double the displayed rate.

cards.front: How does a monitor derive respiratory rate, and why is it unreliable?
cards.back: By impedance — measuring resistance change between chest electrodes as the chest expands. Talking, shivering and movement all register as breaths, making it the least trustworthy number on the screen.

cards.front: What are the usual bedside monitor color conventions?
cards.back: Green heart rate and ECG, blue or cyan SpO2, red or pink NIBP, yellow or white respiratory rate, white or grey temperature. They vary by vendor, so learn your own department's screen.

cards.front: What four steps set a patient up on the monitor correctly?
cards.back: Prep and place ECG electrodes, put the SpO2 probe on a warm perfused site, size and apply the cuff, then set alarm limits for this patient rather than accepting defaults. Then record a full baseline set.

cards.front: Roughly what proportion of hospital monitor alarms are false or insignificant?
cards.back: The large majority — commonly cited as over 85%. That is what produces alarm fatigue, delayed responses and missed real events.

cards.front: Name four patient types for whom default alarm limits are wrong.
cards.back: Severe COPD (baseline SpO2 near 88%), athletes (heart rate in the 40s), rate-controlled atrial fibrillation, and every child, whose normal heart rate exceeds an adult alarm threshold.

cards.front: When is it appropriate to silence an alarm?
cards.back: At the bedside, after seeing the patient and identifying the cause. Never from the desk, and never as a substitute for fixing what triggered it.

cards.front: What three things may you never do to an alarm?
cards.back: Disable it, turn the volume to zero, or widen the limits so far that nothing can trigger them. An unmanageable alarm is a conversation with the nurse, not a knob you turn.

cards.front: How does a pulse oximeter produce a saturation number?
cards.back: It shines red and infrared light through tissue and reads only the pulsating portion of the signal, so it measures arterial blood. No pulsation at the sensor means no valid reading.

cards.front: What must you check before trusting any SpO2 number?
cards.back: The plethysmograph waveform. A clean, regular wave with a sharp upstroke means a real measurement; a flat or ragged wave means the number is a guess.

cards.front: Why does carbon monoxide poisoning produce a falsely high SpO2?
cards.back: Carboxyhemoglobin absorbs light almost identically to oxygenated hemoglobin, so a standard probe can read `100%` in a suffocating patient. CO needs a CO-oximeter or blood gas.

cards.front: List four common causes of a falsely low or unreadable SpO2.
cards.back: Low perfusion from cold or shock, motion or shivering, dark nail polish or artificial nails, and a blood pressure cuff cycling on the same arm as the probe.

cards.front: Why can a patient in respiratory failure still have a normal SpO2?
cards.back: Increased effort — fast rate, accessory muscles, tripoding — keeps saturation normal until the patient tires. Saturation falls last, when compensation fails.

cards.front: What is a normal end-tidal CO2, and what three things does it depend on?
cards.back: `35-45 mmHg`. It depends on metabolism producing CO2, circulation carrying it to the lungs, and ventilation blowing it off. Break any one and EtCO2 changes.

cards.front: Describe the four phases of a normal capnogram.
cards.back: Flat baseline at zero as exhalation begins, rapid upstroke as alveolar gas arrives, flat plateau ending at the end-tidal peak, then a sharp drop to zero with the next inspiration.

cards.front: What does a shark-fin capnogram indicate?
cards.back: Bronchospasm — asthma or COPD. Obstructed alveoli empty at different rates, so the upstroke slurs and never reaches a flat plateau. It improves as bronchodilators work.

cards.front: What does a sudden flat capnogram at zero mean?
cards.back: No exhaled CO2 at all: a disconnected circuit, a dislodged or esophageal tube, complete obstruction, or cardiac arrest. It is checked immediately, never assumed.

cards.front: What is the standard for confirming endotracheal tube placement?
cards.back: Waveform capnography — a sustained, normally shaped waveform over several breaths. An esophageal tube gives no waveform or a few small deflections that fade.

cards.front: During CPR, what does an EtCO2 under 10 mmHg mean?
cards.back: Compressions are not generating enough blood flow. Push harder and faster, ensure full chest recoil, minimize interruptions, and swap the compressor.

cards.front: During CPR, what does a sudden sustained rise in EtCO2 above 40 mmHg suggest?
cards.back: Return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC). Blood is moving again and delivering a backlog of CO2 to the lungs. Confirm with a pulse check at the next rhythm check.

cards.front: Why does capnography detect apnea faster than pulse oximetry in a sedated patient on oxygen?
cards.back: Supplemental oxygen keeps saturation normal for minutes after breathing stops, while exhaled CO2 changes within seconds of the first missed breath.

cards.front: What does an NIBP machine actually measure, and what does it calculate?
cards.back: It measures mean arterial pressure directly from the point of maximum cuff oscillation, then calculates systolic and diastolic from it using the manufacturer's algorithm.

cards.front: How should a blood pressure cuff be sized and placed?
cards.back: Bladder spanning about `80%` of arm circumference and `40%` of arm width, artery marker over the brachial artery, lower edge `2-3 cm` above the antecubital crease, arm supported at heart level.

cards.front: Which direction does a cuff that is too small err, and which way does one that is too large?
cards.back: Too small reads falsely high. Too large reads falsely low, which is the more dangerous error because it can mask real hypertension.

cards.front: Where may you not place a blood pressure cuff?
cards.back: A dialysis fistula or graft arm, the side of a mastectomy with lymph node dissection, a limb with an infusing IV or PICC line, and an injured or casted limb.

cards.front: When should you confirm a blood pressure manually?
cards.back: When it differs sharply from the last reading with no clinical change, when the patient looks different from the number, when the machine errors or repeats, in atrial fibrillation or shivering, and before any treatment decision.

cards.front: What are typical vitals intervals by ESI acuity level?
cards.back: ESI 1 continuous with documentation every `5 minutes`; ESI 2 every `15 minutes` with continuous monitoring; ESI 3 every `30-60 minutes`; ESI 4-5 every `1-4 hours` and at discharge.

cards.front: Beyond the schedule, when do you repeat a full set of vitals?
cards.back: After any medication that can change vitals, after any intervention, when appearance or complaint changes, before transport off the unit, before discharge, and whenever something makes you uneasy.

cards.front: What do reviews of in-hospital cardiac arrests show about the hours beforehand?
cards.back: Most patients had abnormal vital signs recorded for hours before arresting — usually a rising respiratory rate, falling blood pressure, or a change in mental status. The data existed; nobody connected it.

cards.front: How do you calculate shock index, and what value is concerning?
cards.back: Heart rate divided by systolic blood pressure. Normal is roughly `0.5-0.7`; over `0.9` predicts serious illness and mortality better than either number alone.

cards.front: Why is respiratory rate the most ignored vital sign?
cards.back: It is the earliest marker of deterioration but is routinely estimated, copied forward, or charted as 16 or 18 without counting. Count it for 30 to 60 seconds with a hand on the wrist.

cards.front: What urine output signals inadequate perfusion in an adult?
cards.back: Under `0.5 mL/kg/h` — roughly under `30 mL/h` for an average adult. Kidneys stop producing urine early when perfusion falls, making it an organ-level warning.

cards.front: What does mottling indicate, and where does it appear first?
cards.back: A blotchy blue-purple net over the knees and thighs, from failing peripheral perfusion. Mottling spreading outward from the knee is a strong marker of severe shock and poor outcome.

cards.front: Why is new confusion treated as a vital sign?
cards.back: The brain is highly sensitive to low perfusion and low oxygen, so altered mentation often appears before the monitor changes. Any new confusion or agitation gets reported.

cards.front: Why does a narrowing pulse pressure matter?
cards.back: It shows vasoconstriction compensating for lost volume. A pressure going from `120/70` to `100/85` is a deteriorating patient even though the systolic is still above 90.

cards.front: What does a patient who suddenly wants to sleep during an acute illness tell you?
cards.back: It is often a falling level of consciousness, not rest. Along with a reported feeling of impending doom or a talkative patient going quiet, it is a genuine warning sign.

cards.front: How do you turn a gut feeling into something a nurse can act on?
cards.back: Pair it with a trend, a number and an observation: respiratory rate went 18 to 22 to 26 over 45 minutes, systolic 128 down to 96, and she is less responsive than an hour ago.

cards.front: List the four SIRS criteria with their numbers.
cards.back: Temperature over `38 C` or under `36 C`; heart rate over `90`; respiratory rate over `20`; white blood cell count over `12,000` or under `4,000`, or over 10% bands. Two or more is a positive screen.

cards.front: State the three qSOFA criteria.
cards.back: Respiratory rate `22` or higher, altered mentation, and systolic blood pressure `100 mmHg` or lower. Two or more points identifies infected patients at much higher risk of dying.

cards.front: How do SIRS and qSOFA differ in what they are good at?
cards.back: SIRS is sensitive but not specific, so it flags many well patients. qSOFA is less sensitive for early sepsis but far more specific for a bad outcome, so a score of 2 is a loud alarm.

cards.front: What does NEWS2 score, and what does a single parameter scoring 3 mean?
cards.back: Respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, supplemental oxygen use, systolic pressure, pulse, consciousness and temperature. A 3 in any single parameter triggers urgent review, just as a total of 5-6 does.

cards.front: What is in the hour-1 sepsis bundle?
cards.back: Measure lactate, draw blood cultures before antibiotics, give broad-spectrum antibiotics, start `30 mL/kg` crystalloid for hypotension or lactate `4 mmol/L` or higher, add vasopressors if pressure stays low, and repeat an elevated lactate.

cards.front: Why must blood cultures precede antibiotics?
cards.back: Antibiotics sterilize the blood within minutes, so cultures drawn afterward may never identify the organism or its sensitivities. Cultures go first whenever obtaining them will not meaningfully delay the drug.

cards.front: Give the four-part structure of a rapid response call.
cards.back: Who and where you are; who the patient is and why they are here; the concern with actual numbers; and a direct ask — I need someone at the bedside now. About twenty seconds total.

cards.front: What are the first five actions when you find a patient unresponsive and alone?
cards.back: Check responsiveness and breathing, call for help without leaving the room, check a carotid pulse for under `10 seconds`, start compressions if there is no definite pulse, attach the defibrillator when it arrives.

cards.front: State the adult compression rate, depth and ratio.
cards.back: Rate `100-120` per minute, depth at least `2 inches` and not more than `2.4 inches`, full recoil between compressions, and `30:2` compressions to breaths without an advanced airway.

cards.front: How often are compressors swapped, and why?
cards.back: Every `2 minutes` at the rhythm check, in under `5 seconds`. Measured compression depth and recoil degrade within a minute or two, long before the compressor feels tired.

cards.front: What is chest compression fraction, and what is the target?
cards.back: The proportion of the code spent actually compressing. Aim for over `60%`, ideally over `80%`. Interruptions are the most correctable killer in a code.

cards.front: Where do defibrillator pads go, and what do you avoid?
cards.back: Anterolateral: one right of the upper sternum below the clavicle, one at the left mid-axillary line over the 5th to 6th intercostal space. Dry bare skin, avoiding implanted devices and medication patches.

cards.front: Do compressions stop while the defibrillator charges?
cards.back: No. Compressions continue during charging and resume immediately after the shock. Everyone is announced clear, including the person managing oxygen, before delivery.

cards.front: What is the epinephrine dose and interval in adult cardiac arrest?
cards.back: `1 mg` of `1:10,000` IV or IO every `3-5 minutes` throughout the arrest. Tracking that interval is often the technician's timer role.

cards.front: What are the amiodarone and adenosine doses called for in a code?
cards.back: Amiodarone `300 mg` then `150 mg` for refractory ventricular fibrillation or pulseless VT. Adenosine `6 mg` rapid push then `12 mg` for stable SVT.

cards.front: What is the atropine dose for symptomatic bradycardia?
cards.back: `1 mg` IV, repeated every `3-5 minutes` to a total maximum of `3 mg`.

cards.front: Name four non-arrest drugs on the crash cart and their indication.
cards.back: Dextrose 50% for hypoglycemia, naloxone for opioid overdose, calcium chloride for hyperkalemia or calcium channel blocker overdose, and magnesium sulfate for torsades de pointes.

cards.front: What are the immediate post-ROSC tasks?
cards.back: A 12-lead ECG looking for STEMI, blood pressure support with frequent cycling, temperature measurement and targeted temperature management, airway and capnography confirmation, extra access and labs, then monitored transport to cath lab or ICU.

cards.front: What does the RASS scale measure, and what is the usual target?
cards.back: Depth of sedation and agitation, from `+4` combative to `-5` unarousable. Most sedated emergency department patients are targeted around `0 to -2`, drowsy but rousable.

cards.front: A ventilator alarms. What is your role?
cards.back: Look at the patient, check obvious causes such as biting, kinked tubing, secretions or a disconnection, and call respiratory therapy and the nurse. Never change ventilator settings.

cards.front: What monitoring does a patient in restraints require?
cards.back: An order, circulation checks distal to each restraint, skin checks, range of motion, offered food, fluids and toileting, and documentation at policy interval — commonly every `15 minutes` for violent restraint. Never left unobserved.

cards.front: What are the components and range of the Glasgow Coma Scale?
cards.back: Eye opening `1-4`, verbal response `1-5`, motor response `1-6`, totaling `3` to `15`. A drop of `2` or more points is reported immediately.

cards.front: What is the neuro check schedule after thrombolytics for stroke?
cards.back: Neuro checks and blood pressure every `15 minutes` for the first 2 hours, every 30 minutes for 6 hours, then hourly, with blood pressure held under a strict ceiling, commonly `180/105`.

cards.front: What does new headache or vomiting after thrombolytics mean?
cards.back: Intracranial hemorrhage until proven otherwise. Sudden hypertension or any decline in the neuro exam counts the same way. Stop and get the nurse immediately.

cards.front: Why is bradycardia in a child an emergency?
cards.back: A child's heart slows because oxygen delivery is failing, not from cardiac causes. Bradycardia in a child is hypoxia until proven otherwise and is a pre-arrest sign.

cards.front: Why is hypotension a late finding in children?
cards.back: Children maintain blood pressure by clamping down peripherally until they suddenly cannot. Tachycardia, poor perfusion, delayed cap refill and lethargy all appear first.

cards.front: Which patients do you never leave alone?
cards.back: Anyone suicidal or on psychiatric hold, anyone restrained, anyone sedated or not fully awake, anyone with an unprotected airway or vomiting, a seizing patient, and an unstable patient awaiting transport.

quiz.q: The monitor displays a respiratory rate of 34 on a patient who is talking comfortably on the phone. What should you do?
choices: Report impending respiratory failure
Count the respirations yourself for 30 to 60 seconds
Apply a non-rebreather mask
Increase the respiratory alarm limit
quiz.why: Impedance-derived respiratory rate counts chest wall motion, so speech and movement inflate it. Counting by hand is the confirmation step. Acting on the displayed number or widening the limit both skip verification.

quiz.q: A COPD patient's documented baseline SpO2 is 88% and the monitor alarms continuously at that value. What is the correct action?
choices: Disable the SpO2 alarm
Remove the probe until the provider arrives
Ask the nurse to adjust the low SpO2 limit for this patient and document the change
Silence the alarm from the central station each time it fires
quiz.why: The limit, not the alarm, is wrong for this patient's physiology. Disabling the alarm or removing the probe leaves him unmonitored, and repeated remote silencing means nobody ever lays eyes on him.

quiz.q: Why is alarm fatigue considered a patient safety problem?
choices: It shortens the life of monitoring equipment
Repeated false alarms train staff to ignore alarms, delaying response to real events
It increases documentation time
It causes electrode allergies
quiz.why: When the large majority of alarms are false, response times lengthen and real deterioration is missed. That is a documented cause of patient deaths and the reason alarm management is a national safety priority.

quiz.q: A 24-year-old pulled from a house fire is confused with a headache and an SpO2 of 100% on room air. What is the most important concern?
choices: Anxiety from the event
He is adequately oxygenated and can wait
Simple smoke irritation
Carbon monoxide poisoning, which makes the oximeter read falsely high
quiz.why: Carboxyhemoglobin absorbs light nearly identically to oxyhemoglobin, so a standard pulse oximeter cannot detect CO and reads high. Confusion plus a fire history needs a CO-oximeter or blood gas, not reassurance from a normal saturation.

quiz.q: The SpO2 reads 82% with a flat, ragged pleth waveform on a patient with cold hands who is talking normally. What is the first step?
choices: Warm the hand or move the probe and obtain a clean waveform
Apply 15 L/min by non-rebreather immediately
Chart 82% and recheck at the next scheduled set
Call a rapid response
quiz.why: Without a clean pleth waveform there is no valid measurement, and low perfusion is the classic cause of a false low. Get a real number while still assessing the patient. Charting a bad value or acting on it are both errors.

quiz.q: A patient is breathing 32 times a minute using neck muscles and can speak only three words at a time. The SpO2 is 96%. What does this represent?
choices: A reassuring picture
Compensated respiratory distress — saturation falls last
A faulty probe reading high
Anxiety with no physiologic cause
quiz.why: Work of breathing keeps saturation normal until the patient tires, then it drops suddenly. The normal number is the product of effort, not the absence of disease, and the work of breathing is the finding to report.

quiz.q: What is the normal end-tidal CO2 range?
quiz.why: Normal EtCO2 is 35 to 45 mmHg and normally sits within a few mmHg of arterial CO2. Values below that range during CPR indicate inadequate blood flow from compressions.

quiz.q: Three minutes into a code the EtCO2 reads 6 mmHg. What is the correct interpretation?
choices: ROSC has occurred
Compressions are not generating adequate blood flow
The tube is in the trachea and working well
The patient is hyperventilating
quiz.why: During arrest, EtCO2 reflects the cardiac output your compressions produce. Under 10 mmHg means push harder and faster with full recoil and swap the compressor. ROSC causes a sudden sustained rise above 40.

quiz.q: During CPR the EtCO2 jumps from 14 to 46 mmHg over two breaths. What does the team do next?
choices: Increase the compression rate
Assume the sensor failed and replace it
Check for a pulse at the next rhythm check, since this suggests ROSC
Give another dose of epinephrine immediately
quiz.why: A sudden sustained rise above 40 means blood is moving again and delivering a backlog of CO2, which is the classic ROSC signature. It is confirmed with a pulse check rather than assumed, and compressions continue until then.

quiz.q: A blood pressure cuff that is too large for the patient's arm will:
choices: Read falsely low, potentially masking hypertension
Read falsely high
Refuse to inflate
Have no effect on accuracy
quiz.why: An oversized bladder compresses the artery at a lower pressure, so the reported value is too low. A cuff that is too small reads falsely high. The oversized error is more dangerous because it hides real hypertension.

quiz.q: A patient has a left arm dialysis fistula and an IV infusing in the right forearm. Where do you take the blood pressure?
choices: The fistula arm, since a cuff is brief
Stop the IV and use the right arm
An appropriately sized cuff on the thigh or calf, documented
Skip it and chart unable to obtain
quiz.why: A fistula or graft arm is never cuffed, and cuffing over an infusing IV interrupts the infusion and corrupts the reading. A correctly sized lower extremity cuff is the standard alternative, with the site documented so later readings compare fairly.

quiz.q: An ESI level 2 patient is on continuous monitoring. How often should a documented full set of vital signs be obtained?
choices: Every 15 minutes
Every hour
Every 2 hours
Only at triage and discharge
quiz.why: ESI 2 marks a high-risk emergent patient, monitored continuously with sets documented about every 15 minutes. Hourly or longer intervals belong to lower acuity levels, and intervals shorten whenever the patient changes.

quiz.q: A patient's heart rate is 118 and systolic blood pressure is 112. What is the shock index and what does it indicate?
choices: About 0.95 — normal for an adult
About 1.05 — elevated, suggesting compensated shock
About 1.05 — reassuring because the systolic is above 90
It cannot be calculated without a diastolic value
quiz.why: Shock index is heart rate divided by systolic pressure: 118 divided by 112 is about 1.05. Normal is roughly 0.5 to 0.7 and anything over 0.9 predicts serious illness, even when both individual numbers look nearly acceptable.

quiz.q: Which finding is the earliest and most frequently overlooked sign of clinical deterioration?
choices: A falling blood pressure
A rising respiratory rate
A falling SpO2
A rising temperature
quiz.why: Respiratory rate climbs before heart rate and blood pressure change, but it is routinely estimated or copied forward as a normal-looking number. Blood pressure and saturation are late findings, and fever is neither sensitive nor early.

quiz.q: Over four rechecks a patient's blood pressure reads 132/78, then 124/76, then 112/74, then 104/72, with heart rate rising from 88 to 112. All values are within alarm limits. What is happening?
choices: Normal variation that needs no action
A trend of compensated shock that should be escalated now
A cuff size problem
Improvement, since the diastolic is falling
quiz.why: A steady fall in systolic with a rising heart rate is compensated shock, and the shock index has crossed 1.0. Alarm limits are set to catch crises, not trends, which is exactly why the person taking the sets has to connect them.

quiz.q: What urine output threshold suggests inadequate organ perfusion in an adult?
choices: Under 2 mL/kg/h
Under 1.5 mL/kg/h
Under 0.5 mL/kg/h, roughly under 30 mL/h
Under 100 mL/h
quiz.why: Kidneys reduce urine production early when perfusion falls, so under 0.5 mL/kg/h is a recognized organ-level warning. The higher thresholds listed are normal or above-normal outputs.

quiz.q: A patient with a suspected pneumonia has a respiratory rate of 26, is newly confused, and has a systolic of 96. What is the qSOFA score and what does it mean?
choices: 1 — low risk
2 — moderate concern, recheck in an hour
3 — high risk of death, escalate immediately
0 — sepsis is excluded
quiz.why: One point each for respiratory rate 22 or higher, altered mentation, and systolic 100 or lower gives 3 of 3. Two or more marks markedly elevated mortality risk and requires escalation now, not a delayed recheck.

quiz.q: Which set of findings meets SIRS criteria?
choices: Temperature 37.2 C, heart rate 84, respiratory rate 16
Temperature 38.6 C, heart rate 104, respiratory rate 24
Temperature 37.0 C, heart rate 88, respiratory rate 18
Temperature 36.5 C, heart rate 72, respiratory rate 14
quiz.why: SIRS needs two or more of temperature over 38 C or under 36 C, heart rate over 90, respiratory rate over 20, or an abnormal white count. The second set meets three. The others meet none.

quiz.q: In a sepsis workup, the nurse is about to hang antibiotics and the blood cultures have not been drawn. What do you say?
choices: Nothing; antibiotic timing is the only thing that matters
Ask whether cultures should be drawn first, since antibiotics can sterilize the blood within minutes
Suggest cancelling the cultures entirely
Suggest drawing cultures an hour after the antibiotics
