quiz.why: Cultures drawn after antibiotics may never grow the organism, losing the chance to narrow therapy. They go first whenever obtaining them does not meaningfully delay the drug, which is a core part of the hour-1 bundle.

quiz.q: You are activating a rapid response. Which phrasing is correct?
choices: Room 8 seems a little off, come when you can
This is the ED tech, room 8, 64-year-old with abdominal pain: respiratory rate 28, systolic 88, temp 38.9, new confusion. I need someone at the bedside now
Room 8 has been complaining all morning
Can somebody look at room 8 eventually?
quiz.why: A rapid response call must be short, specific and unambiguous: who and where, the patient, the numbers, and a direct ask. Softened phrasing gets the patient deferred, which is the failure mode the system exists to prevent.

quiz.q: You find a patient unresponsive and alone, with occasional gasping. What do you do?
choices: Leave to find the nurse, then return
Give two rescue breaths and wait for a response
Treat gasping as not breathing: call for help without leaving, check a pulse for under 10 seconds, and start compressions if there is none
Wait for the monitor to alarm before acting
quiz.why: Agonal gasping is not breathing and is a cardiac arrest sign. Help is summoned from the room by code button or shouting so compressions are not delayed, and the pulse check is capped at 10 seconds.

quiz.q: What are the correct adult chest compression rate and depth?
choices: 100-120 per minute, at least 2 inches and no more than 2.4 inches
80-100 per minute, 1 to 1.5 inches
120-140 per minute, 3 inches
As fast and deep as possible
quiz.why: Current AHA guidance is 100 to 120 per minute at 2 to 2.4 inches with full recoil. Slower or shallower compressions produce inadequate flow, and excessive depth or rate causes injury and incomplete refilling.

quiz.q: The defibrillator is charging during a code. What happens to compressions?
choices: They stop as soon as charging begins
They continue during charging and resume immediately after the shock
They stop for 30 seconds after the shock to assess
They stop while the rhythm is analyzed and do not resume until a pulse returns
quiz.why: Minimizing interruptions is the highest-yield correctable factor in a code, so compressions continue while the device charges and restart the instant the shock is delivered. Pauses after a shock waste the perfusion pressure just built.

quiz.q: What is the epinephrine dosing interval in adult cardiac arrest?
choices: 1 mg every 10 minutes
1 mg once only
1 mg every 3 to 5 minutes
0.3 mg every 5 minutes
quiz.why: Epinephrine 1 mg of 1:10,000 is given IV or IO every 3 to 5 minutes throughout the arrest. The 0.3 mg dose is intramuscular epinephrine for anaphylaxis, a different drug concentration and route entirely.

quiz.q: ROSC is achieved after a witnessed arrest. Which task is the priority for the technician?
choices: Remove the defibrillator pads
Obtain a 12-lead ECG and support monitoring and blood pressure cycling
Move the patient to a quieter room
Discontinue capnography
quiz.why: Post-ROSC care hunts for a STEMI that caused the arrest and supports perfusion, so the 12-lead and continued monitoring come first. Pads stay on because re-arrest is common, and capnography continues to confirm the airway.

quiz.q: A high-pressure alarm sounds on an intubated, sedated patient. What is the technician's correct action?
choices: Adjust the ventilator pressure limit
Disconnect the circuit to release pressure
Assess the patient for biting, kinked tubing or secretions, then call respiratory therapy and the nurse
Silence the alarm and document it
quiz.why: Ventilator settings are changed only by respiratory therapy or a provider. The technician assesses the patient, identifies obvious mechanical causes, and escalates. Disconnecting or silencing endangers the patient directly.

quiz.q: A 2-year-old with bronchiolitis has had a heart rate of 165 for an hour. It is now 68 and he is limp. What does this mean?
choices: He is finally resting comfortably
The monitor is undercounting
Bradycardia in a child means hypoxia until proven otherwise — this is a pre-arrest emergency
It is a normal range for a toddler
quiz.why: Normal toddler heart rate is roughly 90 to 150. Children slow only when oxygen delivery fails, so a falling rate in a sick, limp child is a pre-arrest sign requiring immediate help, never a sign of improvement.

quiz.q: Ninety minutes after receiving thrombolytics for an ischemic stroke, a patient develops a sudden severe headache, vomits, and becomes drowsy. What is the concern and what do you do?
choices: A migraine; dim the lights and recheck in an hour
Nausea from the medication; ask about an antiemetic
Dehydration; offer fluids
Intracranial hemorrhage; stop and get the nurse immediately
quiz.why: New headache, vomiting, sudden hypertension or any neuro decline after thrombolytics is bleeding into the brain until proven otherwise, which is exactly why checks run every 15 minutes for the first 2 hours. Every other option delays an emergency.

scenarios.title: Room 8: four sets of vitals nobody connected
scenarios.intro: You are covering the B-side hallway. Room 8 is a 64-year-old woman brought in three hours ago for lower abdominal pain and nausea. She is ESI 3, waiting on a CT with contrast. Her triage set was heart rate 88, blood pressure 132/78, respiratory rate 18, temperature 37.4 C, SpO2 98% on room air. The nurse is tied up with a trauma in bay 1.

steps.prompt: It is time for her hourly recheck. She is awake, says the pain is about the same, and asks for a blanket because she feels cold. The monitor auto-cycles the cuff while you are in the room.

choices.text: Count her respirations for a full 30 seconds yourself, note the temperature is now 38.1 C, and chart the set with the trend
choices.feedback: Correct. The impedance respiratory rate is unreliable, and a temperature crossing 38 C in a patient with abdominal pain is a new finding. You have just recorded the first two SIRS criteria.

choices.text: Chart the monitor's numbers as displayed and get the blanket
choices.feedback: The blanket is kind, but a copied respiratory rate is the exact habit that loses a deteriorating patient. Count it, and notice that feeling cold with a temperature of 38.1 C is a rigor, not a comfort problem.

choices.text: Chart respiratory rate 18 because that is what it was at triage and she looks comfortable
choices.feedback: Charting a number you did not measure creates a false flat trend that hides the deterioration from everyone downstream. This is documentation fraud with clinical consequences.

choices.text: Skip the set because the CT will be done soon and vitals can wait
choices.feedback: Deterioration does not pause for imaging. An ESI 3 patient gets a set every 30 to 60 minutes, and a patient about to leave the department for a scan needs a set before transport specifically.

steps.prompt: Forty minutes later. She has been back from CT for ten minutes. She is quieter than before and answers you a beat slowly, but she is oriented. Her hand feels cool and slightly damp.

choices.text: Recognize the trend — rate climbing, pressure falling, respiratory rate 26, temp rising, cool clammy skin — and go tell the nurse now with the numbers
choices.feedback: Right. Shock index is 116 divided by 106, about 1.1. She now meets three SIRS criteria and has diaphoresis and a subtle mental status change. Every one of those alone is a maybe; together they are a pattern.

choices.text: Chart it and wait for the next scheduled recheck, since every value is still inside the alarm limits
choices.feedback: Alarm limits exist to catch crises, not trends. This is precisely the point at which she is still easy to rescue and precisely the point where she is most often missed.

choices.text: Get another blanket and chart that she is resting
choices.feedback: Cool, clammy skin in a febrile patient is a catecholamine surge, not cold. Charting resting converts a warning sign into reassurance in the record.

choices.text: Recheck the blood pressure manually to confirm it before reporting
choices.feedback: Reasonable and quick, and a manual confirmation is good practice before a treatment decision. But do not let it delay the report — say the trend to the nurse while you cycle the cuff.

steps.prompt: The nurse is at the bedside of the trauma patient with her back to you, gloved, holding pressure on a wound. You have about ten seconds of her attention.

choices.text: Room 8: HR 88 to 116, systolic 132 down to 106, RR 18 to 26, temp 38.4, cool and clammy, slower to answer. Shock index is over 1. I think she needs you or the doc now.
choices.feedback: Exactly right. Location, trend, numbers, observation, and a direct ask. That takes twelve seconds and is nearly impossible to defer or misinterpret.

choices.text: Room 8 doesn't look great, whenever you get a chance
choices.feedback: Softened phrasing gets the patient queued behind everything else. The nurse has no numbers to weigh against the bleeding patient in front of her, so she has to guess, and she will guess wrong.

choices.text: Wait until she is finished with the trauma patient so you do not interrupt
choices.feedback: Interrupting is exactly what this information deserves. Ten seconds of a nurse's attention costs the trauma patient nothing and may save room 8 an hour of decline.

choices.text: Tell the charge nurse or the nearest provider instead, with the same numbers
choices.feedback: Good adaptation. When the assigned nurse is physically committed, the information goes to the next available clinician rather than waiting. Just make sure the assigned nurse hears it too.

steps.prompt: The physician comes in, looks at her, and says sepsis, probable urinary source, start the bundle. Orders: blood cultures times two, lactate, CBC, chemistry, urinalysis, two large-bore IVs, fluids, and antibiotics. The nurse asks what you can do.

choices.text: Start a large-bore IV, draw blood cultures from two sites plus the lactate before antibiotics hang, and put her on continuous monitoring with 15-minute vitals
choices.feedback: Correct on every count. Cultures precede antibiotics, the lactate drives the fluid decision, and her acuity just moved to ESI 2, which means continuous monitoring and documented sets every 15 minutes.

choices.text: Hang the antibiotics first since time to antibiotics drives mortality, then draw cultures
choices.feedback: The instinct about time is right, but antibiotics sterilize the blood within minutes and the cultures may then never identify the organism. Cultures go first whenever drawing them will not meaningfully delay the drug.

choices.text: Draw everything off the new IV start and leave her on the same hourly vitals schedule
choices.feedback: Drawing off a fresh IV start is acceptable, but leaving her on an hourly schedule is not. She is now an ESI 2 septic patient and needs continuous monitoring with documented sets every 15 minutes.

choices.text: Get the IV and let the nurse handle cultures later once the patient is more stable
choices.feedback: There is no later. The hour-1 bundle clock started when sepsis was suspected, and cultures drawn after antibiotics lose their value permanently.

scenarios.debrief: Nothing in this case ever triggered an alarm. Every single value stayed inside default limits until she was already in septic shock — which is the entire point. **Deterioration is a trend, and trends are invisible to alarm limits.** The sequence that mattered was heart rate 88 to 104 to 116 to 122 while systolic fell 132 to 118 to 106 to 98: a shock index crossing 1.0 while both numbers still looked survivable in isolation. Layered on top were a counted respiratory rate climbing 18 to 28, a temperature crossing 38 C, cool clammy skin, and a patient who got quieter. The other half of the case is the sentence you say. Trend plus number plus observation plus a direct ask takes twelve seconds and cannot be deferred; something feels off can be, and will be. Then the bundle rules hold: cultures before antibiotics, lactate early, and an acuity upgrade means a new monitoring interval, not the old one.

scenarios.title: Code blue, and you are first in the room
scenarios.intro: 14:52. You go into room 14 to take a set of vitals on a 58-year-old man admitted two hours ago for weakness and nausea. He was awake and talking at his last check 25 minutes ago. The room is otherwise empty; the hallway outside is busy. He is slumped to one side of the stretcher with his eyes closed and you hear a slow, irregular gasp.

steps.prompt: You shout his name and shake his shoulder. No response. He gasps again, roughly every eight seconds. The monitor in the room is not attached to him.

choices.text: Hit the code button in the room and shout for help without leaving, then check a carotid pulse for no more than 10 seconds
choices.feedback: Correct. Agonal gasping is not breathing. Help is summoned from inside the room so nothing delays compressions, and the pulse check is capped at 10 seconds.

choices.text: Run to the nursing station to get the nurse
choices.feedback: Never leave the patient to find help when there is a call button and a hallway full of people. Every second out of the room is a second without compressions.

choices.text: Attach the monitor leads first so you know what rhythm he is in
choices.feedback: The rhythm does not change the first action. Pulselessness does, and you find that with your fingers in under 10 seconds. Leads go on once help and compressions are underway.

choices.text: Give two rescue breaths first to see if he responds
choices.feedback: Current guidance is compressions first in adult arrest. Breaths before establishing pulselessness and starting compressions delay the intervention that matters most.

steps.prompt: No carotid pulse in 10 seconds. You have hit the code button. He is on a soft stretcher mattress with the head of the bed elevated about 30 degrees.

choices.text: Drop the head of the bed flat, slide the backboard under him if it is within reach, and start compressions immediately at 100-120 per minute, at least 2 inches deep
choices.feedback: Right, and in that order. A flat firm surface transmits force to the chest instead of into the mattress. If the board is not immediately at hand, start compressing now and board him during a later pause.

choices.text: Wait for the code team so compressions can start on a proper backboard
choices.feedback: Never wait. Survival falls with every minute without compressions. Imperfect compressions started now beat perfect compressions started in ninety seconds.

choices.text: Start compressions on the mattress with the head of bed still up
choices.feedback: Better than waiting, and starting was the right instinct, but a soft surface and an elevated head absorb your force. Flatten the bed as your first compression begins; it costs no time.

choices.text: Move him to the floor first for a hard surface
choices.feedback: The delay and the risk of moving a patient alone outweigh the benefit. Flatten the bed and use a backboard; floor transfers are not routine for an inpatient stretcher.

steps.prompt: 14:54. You are compressing. The nurse arrives, then the code team floods in: a physician, a second nurse, respiratory therapy, a pharmacist, another technician. The physician takes the head of the bed and says who is on compressions and how long.

choices.text: Call out that you have been compressing about 90 seconds, keep going, and say you will need a swap at the 2-minute rhythm check
choices.feedback: Exactly. The leader needs to know the compression clock to plan the swap, and announcing it yourself keeps the cycle on time without anyone having to ask twice.

choices.text: Stop and step back to let the clinical team take over
choices.feedback: Stopping compressions to hand off outside a rhythm check is an unnecessary interruption. Keep compressing and swap at the 2-minute mark, in under 5 seconds.

choices.text: Keep compressing silently so you do not interrupt the leader
choices.feedback: Codes run on spoken information. Silence forces the leader to ask, which costs more attention than your two-second answer would have.

choices.text: Keep compressing and call out the time you found him down and that gasping was present
choices.feedback: Also valuable. Witnessed arrest with agonal respirations and a known down time changes the leader's expectations and decisions, and you are the only person who has that information.

steps.prompt: 14:56. At the rhythm check the monitor shows coarse ventricular fibrillation. The physician calls for a shock and asks you to take the pads and the timer role. Respiratory therapy has placed an advanced airway and capnography now reads 9 mmHg.

choices.text: Place pads anterolateral on dry bare skin, keep compressions going while the device charges, call clear including the oxygen, then track 2-minute cycles and the epinephrine clock
choices.feedback: Correct in full. Compressions continue during charging, everyone including the person managing oxygen is cleared before delivery, and the timer role is what keeps epinephrine at 3 to 5 minutes and swaps on schedule.

choices.text: Report the end-tidal of 9 out loud and call for improved compression depth and an earlier compressor swap
choices.feedback: Also exactly right. Under 10 mmHg means the compressions are not moving enough blood, and saying that number out loud is the most useful feedback anyone in the room can give.

choices.text: Pause compressions while you position the pads carefully to avoid a misplacement
choices.feedback: Pads go on during ongoing compressions. Any pause you can avoid is a pause you avoid, and pad placement does not require a still chest.

choices.text: Stand back after the shock and wait several seconds to see whether a rhythm appears
choices.feedback: Compressions resume immediately after the shock, without a pause to look. The perfusion pressure built by the last two minutes collapses in seconds, and the rhythm is reassessed at the next scheduled check.

scenarios.debrief: The first two minutes belonged entirely to you, and they are almost all the survival benefit in this case. The pattern: **gasping is not breathing, help is called from inside the room, the pulse check is capped at 10 seconds, and compressions start on a flat firm surface immediately.** Once the team arrives, the technician's value is in three things — high-quality compressions at 100-120 per minute and 2 to 2.4 inches with full recoil, honest information spoken out loud (compression clock, down time, end-tidal), and disciplined role work. Every decision in the second half was a version of the same rule: **do not interrupt compressions.** Not to hand off, not to place pads, not to look at the monitor after a shock. Compressions continue while the defibrillator charges and restart the instant it fires, and the capnography number under 10 mmHg is the room's honest scorecard on whether the work is doing anything at all.
